> However, I found no information of CVI.

Past research has found CVI to perform very poorly.  ECVI performs better.

> There was only information about ECVI with ECVI = NA.

ECVI was only defined for a restricted set of conditions, so it will come up as NA when those conditions aren't met (e.g., for multigroup models).  ECVI is linearly proportional to AIC, so they always provide the same rank order of competing models.  That might be a reason ECVI resarch just kind of stopped (because there was so much AIC research and ECVI doesn't provide any additional information).  So if you are using a likelihood-based estimator, you can just use AIC.

messages.subject: Re: Standardised estimates in a CFA
messages.body_plain:
Yes, you typically want to read the Std.all column, because it standardizes the coefficients in terms of both the predictors (latent common factors) and outcomes (indicators).  So standardized regressions indicate how many SDs the outcome changes when the predictor increases by 1 SD.  When the outcome only has 1 predictor, then the standardized slope is the same as the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient (typically depicted r), but if there are multiple predictors of the outcome, then the standardized slope is a semipartial (or "part") correlation.

Standardized covariances are correlations.  If the variable is endogenous (predicted by something else in the model), then it is the correlation with that variable's residuals (i.e., with the predictor "partialed out").  If both the variables have the same predictor, then their residual correlation is equivalent to a partial correlation (i.e., the correlation after the predictor is partialed out of both outcomes).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Explained Variance with R²?
messages.body_plain:
> Does the rsquare (R^2/R²) show me the variance for a factor/variable that is explained by the model?
> So that a value about .8 or higher indicates a good prediction by the model?

R-squared is the proportion of variance in an outcome the is explained by all predictors of that outcome.  In the case of CFA, the outcomes are the indicators, which are caused by the common factor.  If you also have (observed or latent) variables predicting a common factor, then you will also have an R-squared estimate of the proportion of common-factor variance that is explained by whatever predicts that factor.  So it is just like regression, but SEM fits many simultaneous regression equations, so there is an R-squared for each endogenous variable.

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

> Any explanation for the difference or reassurance that I can confidently use the lavaan correlation matrix as input to EFA functions would be greatly appreciated.

I don't know whether the "quick two step procedure" implemented in psych is the same procedure that lavaan uses.  But you shouldn't separate the steps of estimating polychorics, then treating them as if they are known values when you estimate an EFA.  Your SEs and fit statistic will both yield inflated Type I error rates.  Luckily, you can use lavaan to do EFA, using a function called efaUnrotate() in the semTools package -- just provide your data and the number of factors, along with any other lavaan options (e.g., names of ordered variables if they are not already of class "ordered" in your data.frame), and it will use the appropriate estimator (DWLS with robust SEs and test statistics).  The output is a lavaan object with your initial solution, which you can pass to the oblqRotate() function to obtain an oblique rotation.

Hello Michael,

It is hard to answer your questions without knowing what are the variables about. Generally speaking, assesment how good model is and interpretation of it are the same as if you run it in Mplus. Even the output is not cardinally different.

1). I'd say that your model fits almost satisfactory enough. Some would say you have too high RMSEA, but not fatally. However, it doesn't answer your question whether the model is reasonable. Your theory shoud have te final say here.

2). Again, it's hard to interpret without knowing what do you study, what the variables mean and how they are coded.

Let's say you measure X. I'd say, that with increase of your age measure (q_age) the initial level of X (the intersept) is on average significantly lower. At the same time, with increase in age the change in X over time (your slope) is significantly bigger. Also you can say that with increase in education variable, intial level of X also rises (although significance is marginal), and X changes more (the slope) if relationship variable is higher. The rest of predictors seem insignificant, but how to interpret it depends on your hypotheses.

I hope it helps.

Best,

independent scholar, Ukraine

The "ordered" class should apply to the vector, not to individual observations in the vector, so don't use lapply on it.

> FD.complete$VictimSev.f <- ordered(FD.complete$VictimSev, levels = 0:2,
>                                    labels = c("none","moderate","severe"))

I'm not sure how lavaan treats (ordered) factors as predictors, but I would guess it just uses the underlying integers and treats it the way it would a fixed predictor.  So I think your "b" effect is estimated on the assumption of a linear effect of the mediator on the outcome.  In other words, your model assumes the same amount of mean-difference in the outcome between groups 0 and 1 as there is between groups 1 and 2.  Is that a reasonable assumption?  Maybe check your group means... I'm not really sure how to get around that in lavaan -- you can't create dummy codes for the mediator to use as a predictor, since it has to be coded as an ordinal outcome in the same model.

messages.body_plain:
This isn't a problem, just a curious observation.

I have discovered a difference in the performance of different versions of lavaan, and I wanted to share it. In my SEM course, the first homework is to reproduce a model from Bagozzi (1980) (attached). The paper includes sample moments--correlations, standard deviations, means. One observed variable (the single indicator of "performance") has a variance of about 44,000, while the variance of other variable are in single digits. That difference in scale creates problems for SEM. (The Mplus manual contains a specific warning about such situations.) The model also includes 2 single indicators. Last year, in demo-ing this kind of problem for my students using lavaan 0.5-17, I did this:

1. Analyzed correlation matrix: Result: no problem
2. Analyzed covariance matrix: Result: nonconvergence
3. Divided the standard deviation of the performance indicator by 100 (which divides its variance by 10,000) and analyze this partly rescaled covariance matrix. Result: nonconvergence.
4. Set nonzero residual variance for the two single indicators in the model (using 10% of the indicator's total variance) and analyzed the partly rescaled covariance matrix. Result: it runs, but obviously estimates are affected by the nonzero residual variances.

I am attaching an edited transcript. Unfortunately, I don't have sessionInfo(), but I ran this in September of 2015. I am attaching an edited transcript and afiles with moment matrices and syntax.

Teresa,
A factor model with three indicators is saturated.  Because you have three first-order factors, the second-order factor does not impose any further constraints.  So, the two models are statistically equivalent.

Your choice of model can be based on theory.  If the second-order factor has a good theoretical justification, then it offers a more informative way to model the data (but he correlated factor model is not wrong).  If there is reason to question the second-order factor model then there may be some other explanation for the factor correlations in the correlated factors model.  For example, the factors may bear direct causal relations to one another.  The correlated factors model is basically agnostic because it does not attempt to explain the factor correlations.

There is nothing lavaan specific to this issue.

Keith Markus

messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan users,

lavaan 0.5-22 has been released on CRAN yesterday (24 Sept 2016).

This update mostly addresses some issues related to the 'new' robust
versions of the CFI/TLI/RMSEA fit indices that were introduced in lavaan
0.5-21 (7 sept 2016).

In lavaan 0.5-21, they replaced the 'old' (so-called 'scaled') versions
of the CFI/TLI/RMSEA fit indices in the output of summary(), while in
the output of the fitMeasures(), both *.scaled (=old) and *.robust(=new)
variants are available.

In lavaan 0.5-22, the old versions return back to their normal
positions, while additional lines are printed for the 'new' robust
versions in the output of summary().

*In addition, it turns out that the 'new' robust values were wrong if
(and only if) the test statistic is of the type "mean.var.adjusted" or
"scaled.shifted". The latter is used when estimator = "WLSMV", the
default estimator in the categorical case!*

When the "satorra.bentler" or "yuan.bentler" test statistic is used
(eg estimator MLM or MLR), then the new robust versions are correct, and
to be preferred over the 'old' scaled versions. See

Brosseau-Liard, P. E., Savalei, V., and Li, L. (2012). An investigation
of the sample performance of two nonnormality corrections for RMSEA.
Multivariate behavioral research, 47(6), 904-930.

Brosseau-Liard, P. E., & Savalei, V. (2014). Adjusting incremental fit
indices for nonnormality. Multivariate behavioral research, 49(5), 460-470.

Correct robust versions when the test statistic is "mean.var.adjusted"
or "scaled.shifted" are not yet considered in the literature, and are
currently under development. They will (hopefully) be included in a next
update.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
> Anybody else have any input on this?  Its hard to think that nobody else on here thinks about how to interpret their SEM results...

This is not a lavaan issue, so you should post your question on SEMNET if you want to see more discussion about this.

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>

Testing model fit has nothing to do with testing individual parameters.  If you are analyzing a set of independent variables (i.e., all their correlations are zero), all your estimated paths should be close to zero, and you would only reject a null hypothesis of zero for as many (on average) as corresponds to your alpha level.  However, the model could still fit perfectly because the model-implied covariance matrix would be close to a diagonal matrix, which would closely match the observed covariance matrix.

messages.body_plain:
On 09/25/2016 05:52 PM, kmarkus via lavaan wrote:
> When I run the 3-factor Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example with
> verbose = TRUE, lavaan prints 37 values of the objective function and
> reports the following.
>
> "
> number of iterations:  35
> number of function evaluations [objective, gradient]:  36 36
> "
>
> I am trying to understand why these numbers differ from one another.
>
> The last two values of the objective function seem consistently equal.
> So, I am guessing that lavaan evaluates the function for the first 36 of
> the 37 printed values, but that the final line simply repeats the value
> from the prior evaluation without re-evaluating.  Thus the number of
> evaluations is one less than the number of values printed.

That is correct. lavaan needs one additional function evaluation, after
the optimizer finishes.

  > I am further guessing that iterations refer to parameter value updates
> that take place between the first 36 printed values, the first value
> being based on the start values.  Thus, there are 35 iterations between
> the fist 36 values (and no iteration between the last two values).

No. Depending on many factors, only a single function evaluation may be
needed per iteration, or many more function evaluations may be needed
for a single iteration. For example, the political democracy example:

example(sem)
fit <- sem(model, data=PoliticalDemocracy, verbose = TRUE)

needs 78 function evaluations, over 66 iterations.

To see the iterations themselves (instead of just the function
evaluations), you can switch on the 'trace' option of the nlminb optimizer:

fit <- sem(model, data=PoliticalDemocracy, control = list(trace = 1))

Now, you see only the 'iterations'. To see both function evaluations and
iterations, use:

fit <- sem(model, data=PoliticalDemocracy, verbose = TRUE, control =
list(trace = 1))

and you will notice that in particular at the beginning, two, sometimes
three function evaluations are needed per iteration.

Yves.

Jarod,
  I will offer two further thoughts to complement the strategies offered by Jeremy and Terrence.  (Careful, I think that there may be a single quote in place of a comma in Jeremy's example).

(1)  When using the paste() strategy suggested by Jeremy, I like to enclose expressions to be evaluated in the eval() function.  This is not necessary and some may consider it excessive but I include it as a form of defensive programming to avoid use/mention errors in the code.

(2) Remember that it is possible to feed a parameter table instead of a model to one of lavaan's model fitting functions.

AA <- '[model syntax]'
BB <- lavaanify(AA)
CC <- lavaan(BB, ...)

Sometimes it is more convenient, and produces more readable and extensible code, to edit a parameter table instead of model syntax.  You can adopt a hybrid strategy of generating a parameter table with lavaanify() applied to template model syntax, and then modifying the parameter table (including variable names).  Alternatively, you can directly construct a parameter table.

DD <- data.frame(
  id=NA,
  lhs=NA,
  op=NA,
  rhs=NA,
  user=NA,
  group=NA,
  free=NA,
  ustart=NA,
  exo=NA,
  label=NA,
  plabel=NA)
DD
newLine <- c(1,'y','~','x',1,1,1,NA,0,'','.p1')
DD[1,] <- newLine
DD

Your choice of strategy might depend in part on both the complexity of the models and the extent to which you anticipate extending and reusing the resulting function.  If you can define n-1 of your models as predictable modifications of the nth model, you might consider making the model syntax for the nth model a parameter to your function, lavaanifying it within the function, and then generating the other models by modifying the resulting parameter table.

Keith Markus

messages.body_plain:
> 2) A more general question: if a path X ~ Y is already in the model, and the modification index for Y ~ X is large, does this suggest to just add the Y ~ X path to the model, thus making the model non-recursive, or is it better to swap the X ~ Y path for the Y ~ X path, thus reversing the direction of the arrow in the original model?

This can happen when you have indirect effects that don't fully capture the linear relationship between variables that are not directly related in the model.  If there are several such predictors that only indirectly affect an outcome, sometimes freeing an arrow in the other direction will be a way to increase multiple model-implied correlations with variables "upstream", but obviously that would make the model nonrecursive (without difficult-to-justify constraints).  General questions like this can be posted on SEMNET:

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

But here is what I tell my students.  Modification indices give stupid advice all the time because they are calculated indiscriminately, without regard to any theoretical implications that are in the mind of the modeler, not the software.  Before inspecting modification indices, you should first inspect correlation residuals:

> resid(fit, type = "cor")

Once you see which relationships are being inadequately accounted for by the model (e.g., which correlation residuals > .10 in magnitude), then YOU are smart enough to figure out which parameters should be considered for inspection (e.g., only one among X --> Y, Y --> X, or X <---> Y).  Once you have chosen which modification indices you will consider for inspection, just pay attention to those.

Hi All, Thanks for your help on this. Jeremy's fix worked, and in regard to Terrence's comment, I used many different IVs and DVs. Was just trying to develop a quick bit of code (starting simple) to extract parameters that I could table. This exercise was, in part, to help me get more familiar with R and also to help me learn more about lavaan.

The final, functional code that I plan to adapt is pasted below, though I'll also take a closer look at the functions mentioned by Keith (thanks!).

lavaan.uv.reg <- function(outcome, predictor, RegData) {
  reg.model <-  paste0(outcome,  " ~ ", predictor, "\n",
                outcome, " ~~ ", outcome, "\n",
                outcome, " ~ 1")
  reg.run <- sem(model = reg.model, data = RegData)

  est <- reg.run@Fit@est[1]
  se <- reg.run@Fit@se[1]
  z <- est/se

  p <- 2*pnorm(-abs(z))

  reg.run.output <- cbind(est, se, z, p)
  return(reg.run.output)
}
